newsitem.title: INDIA: Revival in Indian bank credit seen taking time.
newsitem.headline: Revival in Indian bank credit seen taking time.

text.p: A reduction in cash reserve requirements for Indian banks will trigger a cut in lending rates but a pick-up in loans to industry will be slow and far from spectacular, bankers and analysts said on Thursday.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is widely expected to announce a 1.0 to 1.5 percentage point cut in cash reserve ratios (CRR) for banks in its monetary policy for the second half of 1996/97 (April-March), to be announced on Saturday.
"This (CRR cut) will lead to a cut in prime lending rates," said Subra Subramanian, director at securities firm HG Asia. "But a pick-up in credit offtake will take a while -- two to three months."
"It will lead to reduced lending rates," said Ranjit Shah, a director at Su-Raj Diamonds, a leading diamond export firm. "But this will be also because demand for money is less," he said.
In recent statements, the RBI has been emphasising the need to bring down lending rates against the backdrop of a slowdown in borrowing from industry.

Borrowing has been poor this year. Analysts say this is due to a slowdown in the economy owing to last year's high interest rates. The high rates compelled industry to postpone investment decisions which led to this year's slowdown.

"The key to loan growth is expectations on interest rates," said Sandeep Nanda, head of research at NatWest Securities. He said currently the expectations of lenders and borrowers on the movement of interest rates did not match.
Some top Indian and foreign banks cut their prime lending rates by 0.5 percentage points last month, but only the State Bank of India has reported signs of a credit revival.
Bank credit and deposit figures released by the RBI show a decline in credit and a growth in deposits till September 13.

"Although prime lending rates of major state-run banks have come down by 100 basis points over the last four months, they have not resulted in higher credit offtake," said Prabodh Agarwal, analyst at brokerage firm James Capel B&K.
Many banks are hopeful that borrowing would pick up in the traditional "busy" season beginning October, though there are few signs of it as yet.

Some bankers and analysts believe the increase in demand for credit will be slow and painful. The treasurer at a European bank in Bombay said it was illogical to expect a rise in demand for credit just because funds became cheaper.
"Will companies become profitable because funds are available cheaper by one percentage point?" he asked.
"Companies work on larger margins than that," he said.
The real problem was a slowdown in demand, he said, with signs of a decceleration in many industries and reports of inventory build-ups in cement and steel.

"Given that fund raising by industry has not been adequate last year, a lot of investments have been postponed and, to that extent, working capital requirements will be lower this year," said investment firm Kotak Securities in an October report.
